question.text: Scenario: Karan Singh is advising a manufacturing company that exports automotive components. The following economic changes have occurred simultaneously: (1) RBI has cut the repo rate by 75 basis points over the last 6 months from 6.50% to 5.75%. (2) The Indian Rupee has depreciated 8% against the US Dollar from Rs.82 to Rs.88.50. (3) Global crude oil prices have fallen 25% from $90 to $67.50 per barrel. (4) India's GDP growth has improved from 5.5% to 7.0%. (5) The US Federal Reserve has started cutting rates, weakening the US Dollar globally. (6) WPI inflation has fallen from 6.5% to 3.2%. The company earns 60% of its revenue from exports (invoiced in USD) and imports 30% of its raw materials (also priced in USD). The remaining revenue is domestic, and 70% of raw materials are sourced domestically. Karan needs to assess the net impact on the company. Question 3 of 5: The 25% fall in crude oil prices benefits the company because:

answer.text: Crude oil is the company's primary product
Lower crude reduces transportation and energy costs, improving margins, especially for manufacturing companies
Lower crude prices increase the company's export orders
The company trades in crude oil futures

explanation.text: The Logic: Per page 86, crude oil functions as fuel and as an important global input across industries. Per page 88, falling commodity prices can improve profitability and boost stock valuations. For a manufacturing company, a 25% fall in crude oil prices reduces transportation and energy costs, directly supporting margins. The Trap: The company manufactures auto components, not crude oil. Falling crude does not directly increase export orders, which depend on customer demand. Note: The crude-as-input and commodity-price-to-margin linkage is grounded in pages 86-88. Any specific national-level import-dependence percentages or subsidy-burden claims should be separately verified from a current official source before being relied upon.
